title: Pagination done right
summary: Offset paging, why it slows down and drifts, and keyset (seek) paging.

steps.title: Offset paging and its costs
body: `Skip(n).Take(20)` is offset paging: `LIMIT 20 OFFSET n`. It is simple and supports "jump to page 37". But:
- **Deep pages are slow.** To return rows 10,001 to 10,020 the database still has to walk past the first 10,000. Page 500 costs 500 times page 1.
- **Pages drift.** If a new post is inserted at the top while you read, every row shifts down by one: page 2 repeats the last post of page 1. If one is deleted, you skip one.
**Keyset paging** (also called *seek* paging) remembers where the last page **ended** and asks for what comes after:
With an index on the sort column, every page is a seek straight to `lastId`: page 500 is as fast as page 1, and inserts above do not shift what comes next.

steps.prompt: Two posts arrive while a reader is between page 1 and page 2. What does this print?
code: for (var i = 1; i <= 6; i++) db.Posts.Add(new Post { Title = "P" + i, Score = 0 });
db.Posts.AddRange(new Post { Title = "P7" }, new Post { Title = "P8" });
var keyset = db.Posts.OrderByDescending(p => p.Id).Where(p => p.Id < lastId).Take(3).Select(p => p.Title).ToList();
protected override void OnConfiguring(DbContextOptionsBuilder options) => options.UseSqlite("Data Source=feed.db");
protected override void OnModelCreating(ModelBuilder model) => model.Entity<Post>().HasIndex(p => new { p.Score, p.Id });
steps.explain: Newest first, page 1 is P6, P5, P4. Two new posts push everything down, so offset page 2 repeats P5 and P4. Keyset paging asks for "older than P4" and continues exactly where the reader left off.

steps.title: Keyset on a non-unique column
body: Sorting by a column that is **not unique**, like `Score`, needs a tie-breaker, or rows with equal scores could be skipped or repeated. Sort by `(Score, Id)` and seek past **both**:

The client receives the last row's `(Score, Id)` as an opaque **cursor** (often base64 in the response: `"next": "NTo3"`) and sends it back for the next page. An index on `(Score, Id)` makes each page a seek.

The trade-off: keyset paging cannot jump to "page 37", only go next (and previous, by flipping the comparison). That is exactly what infinite scrolling and APIs need; numbered pages over a small table can stay with offsets.

steps.prompt: What does this print? (Scores: P1=5, P2=9, P3=5, P4=2, P5=9, P6=7, P7=5, P8=1.)
code: for (var i = 0; i < scores.Length; i++) seed.Posts.Add(new Post { Title = "P" + (i + 1), Score = scores[i] });
protected override void OnConfiguring(DbContextOptionsBuilder options) => options.UseSqlite("Data Source=feed.db");
protected override void OnModelCreating(ModelBuilder model) => model.Entity<Post>().HasIndex(p => new { p.Score, p.Id });
steps.explain: In `(Score, Id)` order the posts are P8(1), P4(2), P1(5,1), P3(5,3), P7(5,7), P6(7), P2(9,2), P5(9,5). After the cursor (5, 3) come P7, P6 and P2.

steps.prompt: Why must keyset paging over `Score` also compare `Id`?
options: Several posts can share a score; without the tie-breaker the page boundary is ambiguous, so rows are skipped or repeated
`Id` makes the query use less memory
It is only needed for descending order
steps.explain: The cursor must identify one exact position in a total order. `(Score, Id)` is unique because `Id` is.

steps.prompt: Match the paging style to its property.
pairs: Can jump to any page number, slows down on deep pages
Constant speed with an index, no drift on inserts
A total order: required for stable pages
Lets each keyset page start with a seek
steps.explain: Keyset paging needs a total order and an index that matches it; offset paging needs only a total order but pays for every skipped row.

steps.prompt: A product owner wants numbered page links (1, 2, 3 ... 40) on a small admin table of 800 rows. Which paging fits?
options: Offset paging: it can jump to any page, and 800 rows are cheap to skip
Keyset paging: it is always better
Keyset paging with a random cursor
steps.explain: Keyset paging cannot jump to page 37 without walking the pages before it. For small tables and numbered pages, offsets are fine; for large feeds, APIs and infinite scrolling, use keysets.

steps.title: Keyset paging
prompt: The tests give you `FeedDb` with `Posts` (`Id`, `Title`, `Score`) and an index on `(Score, Id)`. Write
record FeedPage(List<string> Titles, int? NextScore, int? NextId);
FeedPage Feed(FeedDb db, int pageSize, int? afterScore, int? afterId)

returning posts ordered by **score descending, then id descending** (best first; for equal scores, the newest first). With no cursor (`afterScore` null), start at the top. `NextScore`/`NextId` are the last post's values when the page is full, or `null` when there is nothing more (a page shorter than `pageSize`, or exactly the last rows: fetch one extra row to find out).
starter: FeedPage Feed(FeedDb db, int pageSize, int? afterScore, int? afterId)
record FeedPage(List<string> Titles, int? NextScore, int? NextId);

if (afterScore is int s && afterId is int id)
query = query.Where(p => p.Score < s || (p.Score == s && p.Id < id));

hints: Descending order means "after" is *smaller*: `p.Score < s || (p.Score == s && p.Id < id)`.
`Take(pageSize + 1)`: if you got the extra row, there is a next page; return only `pageSize` titles.
